aidb_assessment.novelty: The main conceptual contribution is not a new memory architecture but an evaluation lens: measure constructed memory’s marginal value against direct retrieval and decompose per-query differences into benefit and tax. The faithfulness–accessibility–robustness diagnosis makes that lens more actionable.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The central controlled comparisons are broad and practically consequential, and the paper includes useful baseline and configuration checks. Confidence stops short of high because benchmark subsampling, English offline tasks, configuration modifications, reference dependence, missing variance estimates, and incomplete released artifacts limit generalization and exact verification.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: High for reviewers and system builders. It supplies a strong warning against reporting memory performance without a well-specified RAG control, encourages cost-aware evaluation, and identifies concrete failure channels. Adoption should be as an evaluation protocol and design heuristic, not as proof that memory construction is generally undesirable.

executive_summary: The paper asks whether constructed agent memory adds value beyond retrieval from raw history. Across three conversational-memory benchmarks and three backbones, its controlled tables show that most tested memory systems lose to a two-round hybrid RAG reference, although isolated gains remain. It frames these gains and losses as “memory benefit” and “memory tax,” then diagnoses construction loss, reduced accessibility, and cross-backbone fragility. The central warning is persuasive and practically useful, but generality is constrained by sampled, mostly static English benchmarks, modified baseline configurations, incomplete numerical support for several diagnostic figures, and code/results that are promised rather than supplied.

assumptions: Naive hybrid RAG is an appropriate operational reference for the net value of constructed memory, not a memory-free lower bound in an absolute conceptual sense.
Judge accuracy is an adequate proxy for task correctness; the reported human-agreement check supports but does not eliminate judge bias.
Retrieval Scope makes access opportunities more comparable, although it does not equalize exact inference-token budgets.
Changes made to official memory configurations do not materially disadvantage those systems; the authors provide selected validations, but not a full factorial retuning of every method.
Per-query correctness differences against RAG meaningfully operationalize benefit and tax, even though both quantities depend on the chosen RAG implementation.
key_components: Evaluate flat-store, hierarchical/lifecycle, graph-based, and trained-policy memories against one-round and two-round hybrid RAG.
Run main systems with Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, and GPT-5.6 Luna (low), sharing Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and generally a common reranker.
Align heterogeneous retrieval configurations using Retrieval Scope: the fraction of retrievable-store tokens exposed from retrieval through answering.
Measure answer quality with a Qwen3.6-27B LLM judge and separately track token cost, wall-clock time, LLM calls, and memory-store size.
Trace benchmark gold turns into memory units, compare oracle raw evidence with oracle memory evidence, annotate information loss, replay iterative retrieval, and inspect similarity drift.
Construct memories and answer them with different backbones to assess sensitivity beyond raw-history RAG.
Test transfer of the framing on agent-task experience libraries and video world-model memory carriers.
method.overview: The authors treat chunk-based RAG over raw history as the reference and compare each memory system with it at aggregate and per-query levels. A query solved only by memory contributes to memory benefit; a query solved by RAG but lost by memory contributes to memory tax. Main experiments standardize QA models, judge, embedding model, and retrieval exposure where possible. Diagnostic analyses separate construction faithfulness, retrieval accessibility, and robustness to construction/QA backbone changes. Additional experiments cover benchmark headroom, experiential memory, and video world-model memory.

open_questions: Do memory systems retain a net advantage under live, interleaved write–query workloads where raw-history indexing and retrieval must also be continuously maintained?
How do benefit and tax vary by question type after controlling jointly for retrieval exposure, online latency, total tokens, and offline construction cost?
Would system-specific tuning under a fixed compute budget reverse any of the principal rankings?
How stable are the findings across repeated runs, alternative judges, human evaluation, and independently sampled benchmark subsets?
Can a single controlled world-model architecture vary only the memory carrier while holding generator, training data, compute, and retrieval policy fixed?
Does preserving source pointers eliminate construction loss without erasing the compression, privacy, and forgetting advantages that motivate structured memory?

problem.importance: Without a retrieval control, gains attributable merely to finding raw evidence can be mistaken for gains from constructing memory. This matters because memory construction and maintenance add computation and can discard, obscure, fragment, or distort evidence.
problem.scope: The main study covers personal-agent conversational memory, then tests whether the benefit–tax framing transfers to experiential memory and long-horizon world-model memory. It does not establish universal conclusions for all memory forms or live deployments.
problem.statement: Dedicated memory systems alter raw interaction history through extraction, compression, organization, or learned policies, but their marginal value is unclear when direct retrieval from that same history is not used as a strong control.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Each memory system in its standard configuration, two-round raw-history RAG, and a token-budget-matched union that retrieves memory units and source chunks but does not jointly rerank them.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: A hybrid memory with source-history fallback reduces query-level memory tax without eliminating memory benefit.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired per-query net value against two-round RAG, reported with memory-benefit rate, memory-tax rate, judge accuracy, total tokens, and online latency.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop after prespecified paired confidence intervals show either a reduction in tax with no loss of net accuracy under the same online token budget, or no practically meaningful improvement for all tested systems.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Normal retrieval, oracle memory units, oracle raw turns, and source-linked memory units under identical QA prompts and backbones.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Observed memory tax grows mainly from construction loss on some systems and retrieval accessibility loss on others.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Accuracy gap from oracle raw turns to oracle memory units for construction loss, plus the gap from oracle memory units to normal retrieval for accessibility loss.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop when repeated samples yield stable system-level gap estimates with prespecified confidence widths, or when annotation disagreement prevents reliable separation of the two channels.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Best main-table memory systems versus one- and two-round RAG, all with identical cumulative storage, online token, and latency budgets.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: The ranking between constructed memory and raw-history RAG changes under realistic interleaved queries and multilingual updates.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Time-weighted task accuracy minus total operational cost, stratified by language, query type, history age, and update frequency.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop after the preregistered deployment horizon if rankings stabilize across strata, or earlier if one approach is dominated on both accuracy and cost in every consecutive evaluation window.

Exact reproduction remains incomplete because the promised code/results are not part of the supplied record, some decisive analyses are figure-only, and uncertainty across stochastic or sampling variation is not quantified.

results.context: This is the strongest controlled evidence for negative net value in the retrieval-friendly main benchmark. It does not imply that every memory method loses on every benchmark: the same table contains a few positive cells on PersonaMem-v2 and MINT-Eval.
results.result: Across the main comparison, two-round RAG scored 72.2, 81.4, and 90.0 on LongMemEval-s across the three backbones. Every listed memory method was below it in those columns; deficits ranged from −1.2 to −40.4 points.

results.context: These exceptions support the paper’s dual-edged account: memory is not uniformly harmful, and aggregate comparisons conceal query- and task-dependent benefit.
results.result: The main table also shows consequential exceptions: MemOS exceeded two-round RAG on PersonaMem-v2 by +1.0 and +1.5 with two Qwen backbones, while PlugMem and Mem-T exceeded it on MINT-Eval with GPT-5.6 Luna by +3.3 and +3.9.

results.context: This supplies direct evidence that construction loss varies substantially by system. However, the annotation pools sampled facts across three benchmarks, and the supplied table does not expose uncertainty intervals or per-benchmark breakdowns.

evidence.quote: OpenViking 39.4 9.6 13.0 38.0
we sample 500 raw turns from the corpus of three benchmarks and trace each to its corresponding memory unit(s)

results.result: Human annotation found sharply different preservation behavior: MAGMA had 93.6% no loss and 0.0% no memory unit, whereas OpenViking had 39.4% no loss and 38.0% no memory unit.

results.context: The transfer experiment supports task dependence rather than a universal ranking. Token use also differs greatly, so score-only conclusions should be paired with the table’s resource columns.
results.result: In experiential memory, gains depended on domain: Memp scored 76.1 versus naive RAG’s 73.1 on ALFWorld, but on AppWorld naive RAG scored 22.6 while Memp and ReasoningBank each scored 14.3. G-Memory reached 78.0 versus 69.0 for naive RAG on τ2-Bench.

results.context: This supports the narrower claim that latent and cache memories do not consistently dominate direct past-frame retrieval. It is not a clean component ablation because the compared systems differ beyond memory carrier.
